issue_context.title: @angular/pwa doesn't clean up previous service worker version's cached content
issue_context.body:
# 🐞 bug report

### Affected Package
The issue is caused by package @angular/pwa


### Is this a regression?

No


### Description

I am noticing that with every new version of my application the cache size grows considerably because the Angular Service worker is keeping the previous versions of the application in cache? This means that everytime you release a new version of your application, the new version's resources will be cached for offline use (the expected behavior). However, all of the cached content (scripts, css, HTML, etc) from the previous versions of the application are still stored in cache. This means that the application's cache will grow exponentially with every release of your application.


## 🔬 Minimal Reproduction
1. Setup new CLI project ng new my-pwa-app
1. Add PWA support ng add @angular/pwa --project my-pwa-app
1. Build production version of application and run locally (observe cache size)
1. Make small (non-functional) change to the application (just to change file hashing) - representing a new version of your application being deployed.
1. Build production version of the application and run locally again (NOTE: the cache size will be double what it was before). Repeat steps 4 and 5 and this behavior will continue (cache size will continue to grow, because it is holding onto the previous version's cached files).

**Application cache storage (same content, different version):**
Version 1: 12.2 MB
Version 2: 23.5 MB
Version 3: 32.9 MB
...etc.

## 🌍  Your Environment

**Angular Version:** 11
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1774477/115428812-ca0c3800-a1d0-11eb-9636-7d53636e0e12.png)
comments:
The SW does clean up the unused caches, but it does so when it is [initialized][1] - i.e. when a new instance of the SW is created. After some time of inactivity, the browser will stop the SW and it will create a new instance of the SW when it is needed again. 

You typically don't see this behavior when following the reproduction steps you mentioned above, because you deploy new versions before the SW is stopped by the browser. You can simulate this (to see the caches being cleaned up) by opening the `Application > Service Workers` DevTools panel and pressing the `stop` button next to the active SW. (The next time the SW is started - e.g. when reloading the page - it will clean up any unused caches.)

##
While I think the current behavior is sufficient to ensure caches are cleaned up regularly (except in very extreme scenarios, where you deploy multiple versions is short amount of time), I am not opposed to cleaning up more frequently. But I wouldn't want to have the SW check too frequently (for example, on every request), since that sounds wasteful.

I am going to close this, since the caches _are_ cleaned up and the current behavior in intended, but if anyone wants to propose or work on a specific change regarding when caches are cleaned-up, I would be happy to discuss on a new issue (or review a PR :wink:).

(Also, feel free to continue the discussion below, if anything isn't clear or I've missed something.)

[1]: https://github.com/angular/angular/blob/73824d53371f054b1c3277fbdb0481074a36b710/packages/service-worker/worker/src/driver.ts#L508

Actually...I was investigating another issue today and found out that the SW can indeed (under certain rare conditions) leave behind some caches that will never get cleaned up 😱 😇

Reopening...
Thanks @gkalpak. Can you elaborate on these rare conditions? How rare are they?

Sorry, I missed your comment, @jessicajaniuk. I should totally have posted more details on my investigation 😅
(I was planning on quickly following up with a fix, but got caught up in other stuff 😇)

I have submitted a fix in #42622 (along with other improvements).

review_comments: nit: may be include "namespace" into the class name, like `NamespacedCacheStorage` (so it's more clear what the class does)?

I see how my comment can be confusing as it puts more emphasis on the name-spacing part.

However, the main trait of this versus the native `CacheStorage` is that the returned `Cache` instances have a `name` property (which can be used to more easily delete them, for example).

Therefore, I have a slight preference for keeping the `Named` prefix. I will update the JSDoc comment to highlight that.
I don't feel strongly about it though, so happy to switch to `Namespaced` if you think it is preferable.
That makes sense, thanks @gkalpak 👍 Let's keep the `NamedCacheStorage` version that you have in the PR.
The actual version would be populated by the CLI (by replacing the `0.0.0-PLACEHOLDER` string with a current version), right? If yes, I'd propose leaving a quick comment regarding that.

The version is replaced when building the packages (by the [ng_package][1] and [pkg_npm][2] bazel rules). This is the standard mechanism we use to populate fields/variables with the current version all over the repo (for example, in `package.json` files and `VERSION` exports for all `@angular/*` packages, license banners, etc.).

I could add a comment, but I don't think it would help. It would be a drop in the ocean :smiley:
(For reference, the special `0.0.0-PLACEHOLDER` placeholder is used in ~100 files throughout the repo.)

Maybe we could add some docs on how version stamping works (I couldn't find anything from a quick search).

[1]: https://github.com/angular/angular/blob/a16f82b851c1cf1f5ba8739e574dfbc89a662666/tools/defaults.bzl#L178
[2]: https://github.com/angular/angular/blob/a16f82b851c1cf1f5ba8739e574dfbc89a662666/tools/defaults.bzl#L216
You are right! I think it's ok to keep as it as it's a standard thing that we do across the repo. Thanks for the clarification.

Great comment in the commit message! 👍 
Can we capture this info in the code as well (either as a comment above this line or as a JSDoc for this function)?
Should we make `original` private, so that it doesn't leak and all access happens via API methods of this class?

In some cases, we do need to access the original `CacheStorage` (both in tests and in actual code).
But at least we explicitly access it via the `NamedCacheStorage` instance (instead of directly via the `ServiceWorkerGlobalScope`), so it is clear that it is intentional.
nit: we create an intermediate array here, but if we don't expect this function to be used a lot, it doesn't really matter. Just wanted to double-check :)
Yeah, this aspect is not worth optimizing here.
